Authentication & Session Security

Learn how websites verify identity, maintain sessions, handle passwords and MFA, and where authentication logic can fail.

Beginner24 min reading + practice
Where this fits

Lesson 3 of 4 in Web Security Foundations. Module goal: You can distinguish a login problem from an authorization problem and explain the relevant defenses.

View this course’s curriculum →
OverviewHow it worksThe backgroundReal-world examplesWhat to look forDefensive thinkingPractice

Overview

Authentication answers who you are; authorization answers what you are allowed to do. Authentication normally involves a credential or factor, a verification step, and then a session mechanism that lets the application recognize subsequent requests. Failures can appear in login, password reset, MFA, remember-me features, session handling, logout, or recovery flows—not only in the main login form.

How it works

  • A user submits an authentication attempt, usually over HTTPS.
  • The server verifies the supplied factor against trusted credential or identity data.
  • After successful authentication, the application establishes a session using a secure session identifier or another validated mechanism.
  • Subsequent requests carry the session state, commonly through a cookie, and the server maps it to the authenticated identity.
  • Sensitive state changes such as login, privilege changes, password changes, and recovery should trigger appropriate session lifecycle controls.

The background

Web authentication progressed from simple HTTP authentication and password forms toward cookie-based sessions, federated identity, MFA, passkeys, and modern identity protocols. The larger the authentication surface becomes, the more important consistent session lifecycle and recovery controls become.

Real-world examples

  • PortSwigger's current authentication material covers username enumeration, brute-force defenses, MFA logic, password reset, remember-me mechanisms, and other authentication flaws.
  • OWASP ASVS 5.0 separates authentication and session management into dedicated verification areas, reflecting that proving identity and securely maintaining that identity are related but distinct controls.

What to look for

  • Check whether invalid and valid usernames produce distinguishable messages, status codes, response sizes, or timing.
  • Review login rate limiting and whether recovery or password-change endpoints have weaker controls than the main login.
  • Inspect session cookies for appropriate security attributes and check whether sessions are rotated at important authentication boundaries.
  • Review logout, password reset, remember-me, MFA, and re-authentication flows as separate attack surfaces.
  • Look for state-machine flaws where an application grants authenticated functionality before every required verification step is complete.

Defensive thinking

  • Use HTTPS for authentication and enforce secure transport.
  • Use a well-tested authentication framework and store passwords using modern password hashing rather than reversible encryption.
  • Use generic authentication error responses and sensible abuse controls without creating account-enumeration leaks.
  • Generate unpredictable session identifiers and rotate them after authentication or other sensitive state transitions.
  • Protect session cookies with appropriate Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite settings.
  • Make password reset, MFA, remember-me, and account recovery at least as carefully protected as normal login.

Practice resources

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource’s instructions. Test other people’s systems only with permission.

Choose an Apprentice-level authentication lab and focus on the flawed control, evidence in HTTP traffic, and defensive fix.
